title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

Tom practiced a clever ripple: tap-tap, rumble, BOOM. “It begins like a raindrop,” he announced, “and ends like a hippo sneezing.”

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

The last drumbeat bounced off the lily pads, and Tom’s Golden Tadpole Spoon flashed brighter than the fireflies.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:

Mira peered through the cattails. “Nella? Are you hiding, or are you practicing being a cattail?” At once, she discovered whether Nella was there or away.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. With Nella away, Mira called across the pond, “Frogs, fireflies, and anyone carrying a snack—the concert is beginning!”

Tom thumped the kettle-drum. BOOM! Three frogs leaped, one frog applauded, and a lily pad put both hands over its face. “That,” said Tom, “was only my polite finale.”

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

Tom held up the Golden Tadpole Spoon while the frogs cheered. It wobbled like a tiny brass moon above the booming pond.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Pip sang his moon-song on the floating stage. The notes curled over the water, and even the lantern ribbon seemed to lean closer.

Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Pip sang the moon-song. His voice slipped between the reeds like silver thread. Nobody shouted over it. Even Tom held his drumstick still.

The moon-song ended. For one lovely moment, the pond kept the final note all by itself.

Nella stepped from the cattails as Pip’s moon-song faded. One lantern glimmered beside her still, smiling face.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Tom thumped the kettle-drum. BOOM! Three frogs leaped, one frog applauded, and a lily pad put both hands over its face. “That,” said Tom, “was only my polite finale.”

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

Tom held up the Golden Tadpole Spoon while the frogs cheered. It wobbled like a tiny brass moon above the booming pond.

With Nella away, Mira called across the pond, “Frogs, fireflies, and anyone carrying a snack—the concert is beginning!”

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

The last drumbeat bounced off the lily pads, and Tom’s Golden Tadpole Spoon flashed brighter than the fireflies.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

Pip sang his moon-song on the floating stage. The notes curled over the water, and even the lantern ribbon seemed to lean closer.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Pip’s moon-song floated first. Then Tom added a playful ripple—tap, tap, wobble, BOOM! The frogs cheered for both sounds, and the stage bobbed like it was laughing.

Pip sang the moon-song. His voice slipped between the reeds like silver thread. Nobody shouted over it. Even Tom held his drumstick still.

The moon-song ended. For one lovely moment, the pond kept the final note all by itself.

Pip’s final note rested on the water. Beside the cattails, Nella smiled, and a single lantern made a gold path toward her.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Pip sang his moon-song on the floating stage. The notes curled over the water, and even the lantern ribbon seemed to lean closer.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Pip sang the moon-song. His voice slipped between the reeds like silver thread. Nobody shouted over it. Even Tom held his drumstick still.

The moon-song ended. For one lovely moment, the pond kept the final note all by itself.

Pip’s final note rested on the water. Beside the cattails, Nella smiled, and a single lantern made a gold path toward her.

The cheers faded into chuckles as the reed stage settled beneath its lanterns.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” But Nella was away, so Pip’s invitation waited like a tiny folded boat.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

Tom held up the Golden Tadpole Spoon while the frogs cheered. It wobbled like a tiny brass moon above the booming pond.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Pip sang his moon-song on the floating stage. The notes curled over the water, and even the lantern ribbon seemed to lean closer.

The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Pip’s moon-song floated first. Then Tom added a playful ripple—tap, tap, wobble, BOOM! The frogs cheered for both sounds, and the stage bobbed like it was laughing.

For the concert’s two-part sparkle, the frogs gave Tom the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He shared its shine with Pip by tilting it between them.

Pip sang the moon-song. His voice slipped between the reeds like silver thread. Nobody shouted over it. Even Tom held his drumstick still.

The moon-song ended. For one lovely moment, the pond kept the final note all by itself.

Nella stepped from the cattails as Pip’s moon-song faded. One lantern glimmered beside her still, smiling face.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Tom practiced a clever ripple: tap-tap, rumble, BOOM. “It begins like a raindrop,” he announced, “and ends like a hippo sneezing.”

The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

The last drumbeat bounced off the lily pads, and Tom’s Golden Tadpole Spoon flashed brighter than the fireflies.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert

The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop. Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Tom practiced a clever ripple: tap-tap, rumble, BOOM. “It begins like a raindrop,” he announced, “and ends like a hippo sneezing.”

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

The last drumbeat bounced off the lily pads, and Tom’s Golden Tadpole Spoon flashed brighter than the fireflies.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Tom practiced a clever ripple: tap-tap, rumble, BOOM. “It begins like a raindrop,” he announced, “and ends like a hippo sneezing.”

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

Tom held up the Golden Tadpole Spoon while the frogs cheered. It wobbled like a tiny brass moon above the booming pond.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop. Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck.

Pip sang his moon-song on the floating stage. The notes curled over the water, and even the lantern ribbon seemed to lean closer.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Pip’s moon-song floated first. Then Tom added a playful ripple—tap, tap, wobble, BOOM! The frogs cheered for both sounds, and the stage bobbed like it was laughing.

For the concert’s two-part sparkle, the frogs gave Tom the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He shared its shine with Pip by tilting it between them.

Pip sang the moon-song. His voice slipped between the reeds like silver thread. Nobody shouted over it. Even Tom held his drumstick still.

The moon-song ended. For one lovely moment, the pond kept the final note all by itself.

Nella stepped from the cattails as Pip’s moon-song faded. One lantern glimmered beside her still, smiling face.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Tom thumped the kettle-drum. BOOM! Three frogs leaped, one frog applauded, and a lily pad put both hands over its face. “That,” said Tom, “was only my polite finale.”

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop. Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

Tom held up the Golden Tadpole Spoon while the frogs cheered. It wobbled like a tiny brass moon above the booming pond.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck.

Pip sang his moon-song on the floating stage. The notes curled over the water, and even the lantern ribbon seemed to lean closer.

Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Pip’s moon-song floated first. Then Tom added a playful ripple—tap, tap, wobble, BOOM! The frogs cheered for both sounds, and the stage bobbed like it was laughing.

For the concert’s two-part sparkle, the frogs gave Tom the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He shared its shine with Pip by tilting it between them.

Pip sang the moon-song. His voice slipped between the reeds like silver thread. Nobody shouted over it. Even Tom held his drumstick still.

The moon-song ended. For one lovely moment, the pond kept the final note all by itself.

Pip’s final note rested on the water. Beside the cattails, Nella smiled, and a single lantern made a gold path toward her.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Pip pressed one toe to the mud and listened. Behind the cattails, he discovered that Nella’s hearing was keen. “Then even a whisper can be a concert,” he said.

“I want to play the moon-song for Nella,” Pip told Tom. “It has three soft notes and one enormous feeling.” Tom looked at the drum, which suddenly seemed very enormous too.

Pip leaned toward Tom. “Nella can hear keenly,” he whispered. Tom’s drumstick froze halfway to the sky. “Keenly?”

Tom looked at Pip, then at the drum. “All right,” he said. “Your moon-song first. I’ll make my finale small enough to fit in a frog’s pocket.” Pip beamed; Tom’s drumstick gave a brave little salute.

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck.

Pip sang his moon-song on the floating stage. The notes curled over the water, and even the lantern ribbon seemed to lean closer.

Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Pip’s moon-song floated first. Then Tom added a playful ripple—tap, tap, wobble, BOOM! The frogs cheered for both sounds, and the stage bobbed like it was laughing.

Pip sang the moon-song. His voice slipped between the reeds like silver thread. Nobody shouted over it. Even Tom held his drumstick still.

The moon-song ended. For one lovely moment, the pond kept the final note all by itself.

Nella stepped from the cattails as Pip’s moon-song faded. One lantern glimmered beside her still, smiling face.

title: The Moonlit Pond Concert
story:
The floating stage bobbed beside the bank while Mira planned glittering cheers, Tom polished his drumsticks, and Pip whispered, “A quiet song for Nella.” Nobody yet knew whether Nella was behind the cattails or away.

Pip sent the paper invitation sliding through the cattails, where it landed with a polite little plop.

Tom practiced a clever ripple: tap-tap, rumble, BOOM. “It begins like a raindrop,” he announced, “and ends like a hippo sneezing.”

A hand appeared between the cattails and accepted the invitation. Nella did not step out yet, but one bright eye peeked toward the pond.

Mira and Pip pushed the reed stage onto the pond. It floated proudly, though one corner wiggled like a ticklish duck. Mira draped the lantern ribbon across the stage. The lights blinked on, making the pond look sprinkled with tiny moons. The invitation fluttered, the lanterns glowed, and Mira called, “Welcome to the pond concert!” From the cattails came a pleased rustle.

Tom struck the finale. BOOM-BOOM-BOOM! Frogs cheered, lily pads bounced, and Tom grinned so widely that his ears nearly became parentheses.

The frogs presented Tom with the Golden Tadpole Spoon. He lifted it high; it wobbled in the moonlight like a very tiny trophy moon.

The drum’s last boom rolled away, and Tom tucked the wobbling spoon beside his heart.

The last drumbeat bounced off the lily pads, and Tom’s Golden Tadpole Spoon flashed brighter than the fireflies.
